intro.html: These ten words come in five pairs that look or sound alike but mean different things. Mixing them up is one of the most common slips in writing, and test makers love to check for it. Learn each pair together, with a trick for telling the twins apart.

affect (to influence; a verb) and effect (the result; a noun). imply (the speaker hints) and infer (the listener figures out). elicit (to draw out) and illicit (not allowed). ingenious (clever) and ingenuous (innocent). eminent (famous) and imminent (about to happen).

words.def: to have an influence on; to change
words.ex: Lack of sleep can {affect} how well you do on a test.
words.ctx: The long drought {affected} every farm in the valley: the corn grew short, the wells ran low and the cows had to be moved to greener pastures.
words.etym: From Latin afficere, “to do something to, to act on”: ad (to) + facere (to do).
words.note: Affect is almost always a verb. (In psychology, affect can also be a noun for the feelings a person shows.)

mn.cue: A is for ACTION: you AFFECT
mn.text: Pip taps the first block, and his one small action changes the whole row: his tap {affects} every block down the line.

scene.alt: A boy taps the first block in a row, starting a chain that will knock them all down.

words.def: a result; a change that something causes
words.ex: The new streetlights had a clear {effect}: far fewer people tripped on the dark corner.
words.ctx: Planting trees along the street had a surprising {effect}; the block grew cooler in summer, and more neighbors came out to sit on their porches.
words.etym: From Latin effectus, “a result,” from efficere, “to bring about, to work out”: ex (out) + facere (to do).
words.note: Effect is usually a noun. As a verb it means “to bring about”: to effect a change is to make it happen.

mn.cue: E is for END: the EFFECT comes last
mn.text: Zoe waters her bean plant every day for a month. The end result, a plant taller than she is, is the {effect} of all that care.

scene.alt: A girl cheers beside a giant plant that grew because she watered it every day.

words.def: to suggest something without saying it directly
words.ex: By yawning loudly through the whole movie, Kai {implied} that it was boring.
words.ctx: Mom never said that Dev’s room was messy, but she {implied} it: she handed him a trash bag and a laundry basket and smiled sweetly.
words.etym: From Old French emplier, from Latin implicare, “to fold in, to entwine”: a meaning folded inside the words.
words.note: The speaker implies; the listener infers.

mn.cue: IM-PLY: the hint goes IN the message
mn.text: The café is closing. Jamal yawns and points at the clock; without a word, he {implies} that it is time for the last customers to go.

scene.alt: A sleepy waiter points at the clock to hint that the café is closing, while two customers keep chatting.

words.def: to figure out from clues or evidence
words.ex: From the muddy paw prints on the rug, Lin {inferred} that the dog had come inside.
words.ctx: The card did not say who had left the flowers, but Ada {inferred} that it was her neighbor: the roses matched the bush beside his front door.
words.etym: From Latin inferre, “to bring in”: in (in) + ferre (to carry). You bring in a conclusion from the clues.

mn.cue: in-FUR: she INFERS from the FUR
mn.text: Lin spots brown fur all over the white sofa and figures it out: the dog has been napping there again. From the fur, she {infers} the truth.

scene.alt: A woman with a magnifying glass finds dog fur on the sofa and figures out that the dog has been napping there.

words.def: to draw out a response, an answer or a feeling
words.ex: The clown’s silly walk {elicited} giggles from every child in the room.
words.ctx: The teacher’s question was meant to {elicit} more than a yes or a no; she wanted her students to explain their thinking out loud.
words.etym: From Latin elicere, “to draw out, to lure out”: e (out) + lacere (to lure).

mn.text: Tia pulls a rabbit out of her hat, and the trick draws a gasp out of the crowd: it {elicits} a great big “Ooh!”

scene.alt: A magician lifts a rabbit up high, and the children in the audience gasp and clap.

words.def: not allowed by law or by the rules
words.ex: The camp counselors found an {illicit} stash of candy hidden under a bunk.
words.ctx: The garage looked like an ordinary bike shop, but its back room hid an {illicit} business: stolen bikes were repainted there and sold in the next town.
words.etym: From Latin illicitus, “not allowed”: in (not) + licitus (allowed), from licere, “to be allowed.”

mn.text: The sign says NO CATS ON THE TABLE, but Pepper sneaks up for the fish anyway. Her snack is {illicit}!

scene.alt: A sneaky cat climbs onto the kitchen table for a fish beside a sign that says no cats.

words.ex: Sami rigged an {ingenious} pulley that lowers snacks down to his bottom bunk.
words.ctx: The flood had washed out the footbridge, but the villagers came up with an {ingenious} fix: they lashed empty barrels together into a floating walkway.
words.etym: From Latin ingeniosus, from ingenium, “natural talent, cleverness,” the same source as engine and engineer.

mn.text: Dev’s robot sorts the laundry by color and folds every sock: an idea worthy of a genius. It is {ingenious}.

scene.alt: A proud teen with goggles shows off the clever sock-sorting robot he invented.

words.def: innocent, trusting and open; with nothing to hide
words.ex: With {ingenuous} delight, Theo told the whole family exactly what he had bought Mom for her birthday.
words.ctx: The new student was {ingenuous}, not crafty: when the teacher asked whether she had read the book, she admitted at once that she had only watched the movie.
words.etym: From Latin ingenuus, “freeborn; frank, open”: a person born free, with nothing to hide.
words.note: Ingenuous (innocent, trusting) and ingenious (clever) differ by one letter. Disingenuous means only pretending to be innocent.

mn.text: When the teacher asks who forgot their homework, little Theo’s hand shoots up at once: he hides nothing. He is {ingenuous}.

scene.alt: A small boy cheerfully raises his hand to admit he forgot his homework while his teacher smiles.

words.def: famous and respected in a field
words.ex: An {eminent} scientist visited our school to talk about volcanoes.
words.ctx: Although she had won every major prize in music, the {eminent} composer still taught a free piano class for beginners every Saturday morning.
words.etym: From Latin eminere, “to stand out, to rise above”: e (out) + minere (to jut out).

mn.text: Professor Edwin stands out above everyone in his field, and the crowd rises to cheer him: he is {eminent}.

scene.alt: A famous old professor wearing a medal waves from a podium while teens cheer for him.

words.def: about to happen, often something bad
words.ex: With thunder rumbling closer, the lifeguard warned that a storm was {imminent}.
words.ctx: Dark clouds piled up over the hills and the birds went quiet; everyone at the picnic could tell that rain was {imminent}, so they began packing up.
words.etym: From Latin imminere, “to hang over, to threaten”: in (over) + minere (to jut out).

mn.text: A huge wave is rolling toward Lila’s sandcastle; it will hit in a minute. The crash is {imminent}!

scene.alt: A girl panics as a huge wave rolls toward her sandcastle.

rows: Affect is the Action; the Effect is the End result.
The speaker implies; the listener infers.
after.cap: Five pairs and a trick for each.

after.html: Two exceptions to the affect and effect rule. Effect can be a verb meaning “to bring about”: the new principal effected real change (she made it happen). And affect can be a noun in psychology, for the feelings a person shows. Everywhere else, affect is the verb and effect is the noun: the rain affected the game, and the rain had an effect on the game.

opts.s: The icy wind did not {affect} the penguins at all; they waddled happily across the snow.
opts.why: The blank needs a verb meaning “to influence”: affect.

items.q: The new bell schedule will ______ every class in the school. Which word fits?
items.why: The blank needs a verb meaning “to influence”: affect. Effect is usually the noun, the result.

items.q: From the coach’s huge smile, the team ______ that they had made the playoffs. Which word fits?
items.why: The team figured it out from a clue, so they inferred it. The coach’s smile implied it.

items.q: An ______ child believes whatever she is told and hides nothing. Which word fits?
items.why: Ingenuous means innocent and trusting. Ingenious, with an i, means clever.

items.q: True or false: “Grab your umbrella; rain is eminent” uses the right word.
items.why: False. Rain that is about to fall is imminent (IN A MINute). Eminent means famous and respected.

items.q: The comedian’s first joke ______ a roar of laughter from the crowd. Which word fits?
items.why: To elicit is to draw out a response, like laughter. Illicit sounds the same but is an adjective meaning not allowed.

items.q: True or false: effect can be a verb meaning “to bring about.”
items.why: True. To effect a change is to make it happen. Most of the time, though, effect is a noun: the result.
